Idioms & Slang · Week 8 · Independent Level (A2+ → B1)

Teacher Copy: Problems & Solutions

Week 8 Lesson Plan: Problems & Solutions

Concept: Leo's Rough Week. A funny, neutral story (locked keys, a lost speech, a broken ladder) introduces the five expressions as a "problem rollercoaster". Students then react with empathy, choose the right register, and tell their own bounce-back stories (real or invented).

Syllabus focus

  • Expressions: in a tight spot, back to square one, face the music, turn a corner (taught as turn the corner, both accepted), out of the woods
  • SLO (B1): describe difficult situations and recovery, respond with empathy; find and fix errors (the square one, tightly spot)

Recycled

  • Weeks 1–7 in Back-to-Back Taboo
  • figure out, sort out, start over (Week 3), patch things up (Week 4), pull your weight (Week 7) in role-plays and the Hotline
  • Final core: in a tight spot, turn a corner
Movement activities (3): Human Timeline (Block 1), Problem Wall and Advice Hotline (Block 2).
Materials: student copy (phones or print PDF), Slides tab, Human Timeline strips, 6 Problem Wall posters, sticky notes, 8 Hotline cards, 6 role-play cards (all in Cards tab / Cards PDF).

Block 1 · Engage

Rate the Disaster

1 = no big deal · 5 = total disaster

  1. You lock your keys in your car.
  2. You send a text about your boss... to your boss.
  3. Your phone falls in the toilet.
  4. You forget your best friend's birthday.
  5. You miss the last train home.
  6. You spill coffee on your laptop before an important meeting.
Idioms & Slang · Week 8 · Problems & Solutions
Read each one; students show 1-5 fingers. Ask the 1s and the 5s to explain. Pairs then choose one and say what they would do. Do NOT teach the expressions yet. Listen for natural language: "That's a nightmare", "I'd freak out".
Leo's Rough Week · Monday

in a tight spot

Monday, 5:00 p.m. Leo locks his keys in his car at the grocery store. His phone is at 3%. He has to pick up his best friend at the airport in one hour. Leo is in a tight spot.

Think: Is this an easy or a difficult situation? What does "in a tight spot" mean?

Meaning: in a difficult situation, and it's hard to find a way out (often with little time or money)
Pattern: be in a tight spot · be in a bit of a tight spot
Idioms & Slang · Week 8 · Problems & Solutions
Read the situation dramatically. Ask the Think question, then press R. Before moving on, ask: What goes wrong on Tuesday? Take 2-3 predictions. Key mistake: NOT "in a tightly spot" (tight is an adjective) and NOT "in tight spot" (you need a). Students open the Monday card in the Toolkit tab.
Leo's Rough Week · Tuesday

back to square one

Tuesday. For two weeks, Leo has been writing a wedding speech for his best friend. Tonight his laptop crashes. No backup. The speech is gone. Leo is back to square one.

Think: Does Leo have to start again? What does "back to square one" mean?

Meaning: back at the beginning, because your plan or work failed; you have to start again
Pattern: be back to square one · go back to square one · be back at square one
Idioms & Slang · Week 8 · Problems & Solutions
Read the situation dramatically. Ask the Think question, then press R. Before moving on, ask: What goes wrong on Wednesday? Take 2-3 predictions. Key mistake: NOT "back to the square one" (no the) and NOT "back to square first." Students open the Tuesday card in the Toolkit tab.
Leo's Rough Week · Wednesday

face the music

Wednesday. Last week Leo borrowed his neighbor's ladder and broke it. He hid it in his garage for two days. Now his neighbor, Mr. Kim, is knocking on the door. It's time to face the music.

Think: Whose mistake was it? What does Leo have to do now?

Meaning: to accept the bad results (consequences) of something YOU did wrong
Pattern: have to face the music · it's time to face the music · be ready to face the music
Idioms & Slang · Week 8 · Problems & Solutions
Read the situation dramatically. Ask the Think question, then press R. Before moving on, ask: What goes wrong on Thursday? Take 2-3 predictions. Key mistake: NOT for bad luck: "It rained on her wedding, so she faced the music." (wrong). NOT "face the musics." Students open the Wednesday card in the Toolkit tab.
Leo's Rough Week · Thursday

turn the corner

Thursday. Leo tells Mr. Kim the truth. Mr. Kim laughs: "It was 20 years old!" Then Leo's friend saves half of the speech file. Things are getting better. Leo has turned the corner.

Think: Is Leo's week getting better or worse now?

Meaning: to get past the worst part of a problem; things start to get better
Pattern: turn the corner (most common in the U.S.) · turn a corner (also used)
Idioms & Slang · Week 8 · Problems & Solutions
Read the situation dramatically. Ask the Think question, then press R. Before moving on, ask: What goes wrong on Friday? Take 2-3 predictions. Key mistake: NOT "turned corner" (you need the or a). Use it when things START to improve, not when everything is perfect. Students open the Thursday card in the Toolkit tab.
Leo's Rough Week · Friday

out of the woods

Friday. The speech is finished, the car is fine, and Leo bought Mr. Kim a new ladder. The hard part is over. He's out of the woods. Well... the wedding is tomorrow, so he's not out of the woods yet!

Think: What's the difference between "out of the woods" and "not out of the woods yet"?

Meaning: safe; the difficult or dangerous part is over. Very often negative: not out of the woods yet = better, but there may still be problems.
Pattern: be out of the woods
Idioms & Slang · Week 8 · Problems & Solutions
Read the situation dramatically. Ask the Think question, then press R. Point out the negative form: not out of the woods yet. Key mistake: NOT "out of the wood" (that's British). In American English: woods. Students open the Friday card in the Toolkit tab.

Idioms & Slang · Week 8 · Problems & Solutions
Choral drill, then say it with feeling: worried (tight spot), frustrated (square one), nervous (face the music), relieved (turn the corner), happy (out of the woods).
Block 1 · Concept check

The Problem Rollercoaster

ProblemWorst momentGetting betterSafe
  1. in a tight spot → The problem starts
  2. back to square one → Your plan fails, start again
  3. face the music → You accept the result of your mistake
  4. turn the corner → Things start to get better
  5. out of the woods → Safe! The hard part is over
Idioms & Slang · Week 8 · Problems & Solutions
Part 2. Draw a rollercoaster on the board: down, down, down, up, up. Students place each expression. Press R to check.

Block 2 · Register

The Register Ladder

You are going to miss a deadline. From most formal to most casual:

  1. "Unfortunately, I won't be able to meet Friday's deadline." Formal
  2. "I'm in a bit of a tight spot with the deadline." Neutral
  3. "I'm running a little behind on this." Casual
  4. "Ugh, I'm totally toast. That deadline's gonna kill me." Very casual / slang
Idioms & Slang · Week 8 · Problems & Solutions
Part 8A, then 8B (choose the best sentence) and 8C (slang to recognize). Ask: who would you say the second one to? (Manager: yes, it's neutral.)

  2. back to square one = Your plan fails, start again
  3. face the music = You accept the result of your mistake
  4. turn the corner = Things start to get better
  5. out of the woods = Safe! The hard part is over

Part 5: Human Timeline

Story A: Rosa's Food Truck

  1. Rosa opened a taco truck in Lowell last spring.
  2. In July, the engine died in the middle of a big festival. She was in a tight spot.
  3. The mechanic said the engine couldn't be saved. She needed a new truck. Back to square one!
  4. Rosa had ignored the "check engine" light for months. She had to face the music and pay for it.
  5. In September, a friend lent her money, and a used truck arrived.
  6. By October, she had more customers than ever. She had turned the corner.
  7. Now she saves money every week. She's finally out of the woods.

Story B: Kwame's Moving Day

  1. Kwame found a great apartment in Worcester and planned to move on Saturday.
  2. On Friday night, the moving company canceled. He was in a tight spot.
  3. On Saturday morning, the landlord called: the apartment wasn't ready. Back to square one!
  4. Kwame had forgotten to sign one important form. He had to face the music and call the landlord to apologize.
  5. The landlord was kind and gave him a new move-in date.
  6. With help from three friends, the move went well. Kwame felt he had turned the corner.
  7. A week later, all the boxes were unpacked. He was out of the woods.
Expression order in both stories: in a tight spot, back to square one, face the music, turned the corner, out of the woods.

Part 6: Empathy Upgrade

  1. "Oh no, you're in a tight spot! Can I drive you?"
  2. "Ugh, back to square one. I'm sorry. Want help brainstorming?"
  3. "Thanks for telling me. Don't worry, it was old."
  4. "That's great! Sounds like you've turned the corner."
  5. "I'm glad you're safe. You're not out of the woods yet, so call me if you need anything."
  6. "That's really frustrating. Want to practice together this weekend?"
Your turn (possible): 1 "Oh no, you're in a tight spot! Tell the boss soon. It's better to face the music now." 2 "That's such a relief! Sounds like you've turned the corner."

Part 7: Fix-It Garage

  1. We're back to square one with the project. (no the)
  2. I'm in a tight spot this month. (adjective)
  3. The company is finally out of the woods. (plural)
  4. He knows he has to face the music. (no -s)
  5. After a hard year, we turned the corner. (the or a)
  6. It's time to face the music. (no to)
Bonus: face the music is for the results of your own mistakes. Rain is bad luck, not Leo's fault.

Part 8: Right Words, Right Person

A: "Unfortunately, I won't be able to meet Friday's deadline." = Formal, "I'm in a bit of a tight spot with the deadline." = Neutral, "I'm running a little behind on this." = Casual, "Ugh, I'm totally toast. That deadline's gonna kill me." = Very casual / slang
B:
  1. "Unfortunately, I won't be able to finish the report by Friday."
  2. "Dodged a bullet! Made the flight with two minutes left."
  3. "I'm sorry, I broke the window. I'll pay for the repair."
  4. "Well, we're back to square one with the design."
  5. "We were in a tight spot, but we turned the corner by changing our process."
  6. "I'm sorry, I had a problem with my laptop. Can I send it tomorrow?"

Exit Ticket

1 We are back to square one. 2 No, there could still be problems.

Role-Play Cards (6)

Role-play 1: The Lost Passport

Situation: Two friends. A is traveling to a family wedding in 10 days.

A: You can't find your passport anywhere. You're panicking. Call B.
B: You are calm and organized. Help A make a plan: where to look, who to call, what to do next.

Goal: Make a step-by-step plan together. · Use: in a tight spot · back to square one · figure out (Week 3)
Useful: "I don't know what to do." · "Okay, first..." · "Have you checked...?" · "You'll figure it out."
Challenge: B: ask four questions before giving advice.

Role-play 2: The Broken Promise

Situation: Two friends. Last Saturday, A promised to help B move, but A overslept and never came.

A: Call B. Apologize and offer to make it right.
B: You were upset, and you moved everything alone. Listen. Decide if you can forgive A.

Goal: Apologize and patch things up. · Use: face the music · patch things up (Week 4) · out of the woods
Useful: "I owe you an apology." · "I know I messed up." · "How can I make it up to you?" · "Thanks for telling me."
Challenge: A: don't make excuses. B: say how you felt with one "I felt..." sentence.

Role-play 3: The Landlord Call

Situation: A tenant calls the landlord. It's November, and the heater has been broken for a week.

A: Tenant: the repair person canceled twice. Your apartment is very cold. Be polite but firm.
B: Landlord: you want to help, but the repair company is very busy. Find a temporary solution.

Goal: Agree on a repair date AND a solution for tonight. · Use: in a tight spot · back to square one · turn the corner
Useful: "I'm calling about..." · "This is the second time..." · "What can you do in the meantime?" · "I understand."
Challenge: Tenant: stay polite even when the landlord says "maybe next week."

Role-play 4: Comeback Stories (Podcast)

Situation: A local podcast called Comeback Stories. A is the host, and B is the guest.

A: Host: welcome B and interview them about a hard time and how they recovered.
B: Guest (real or invented: a small business owner, an athlete, a student, a chef...): tell your story from the problem to the recovery.

Goal: Tell the whole story: problem, setback, turning point, today. · Use: all five expressions
Useful: "Welcome to the show!" · "Take us back to..." · "What happened next?" · "What was the turning point?"
Challenge: Host: four follow-up questions. Guest: use the past simple AND one present perfect.

Role-play 5: The Group Project Crash

Situation: Two classmates. Your presentation is tomorrow at 9:00. The shared file won't open.

A: You saved the last version. You think it's your fault.
B: You haven't done your part yet. (Review: Week 7, pull your weight.)

Goal: Decide what to do tonight and who tells the teacher. · Use: back to square one · face the music · pull your weight (Week 7)
Useful: "Okay, don't panic." · "What if we...?" · "I'll take the first part." · "Should we email the teacher?"
Challenge: Agree on a plan in under three minutes.

Role-play 6: The Important Application (optional)

Situation: Two friends. A gets a letter about an important application (school, apartment, job, or another one: real or invented).

A: The letter says you need more documents, and part of the process starts again.
B: Be supportive. Help A see the next steps and stay positive.

Goal: Make a plan and end on a positive note. · Use: back to square one · in a tight spot · turn the corner
Useful: "That's so frustrating." · "At least..." · "What's the next step?" · "You've got this."
Challenge: This card is optional. You can always invent the details.

Problem Wall Posters (6)

PROBLEM 1
I lent my friend $300 for her rent. Now she says she can't pay me back until summer, and my own rent is due next week.
Your advice: empathy first + an expression if it fits
PROBLEM 2
I studied for my driver's license for three months... and I failed. Again. The next test date is in six weeks.
Your advice: empathy first + an expression if it fits
PROBLEM 3
I borrowed my roommate's car and scratched the door. She doesn't know yet. She's coming home tonight.
Your advice: empathy first + an expression if it fits
PROBLEM 4
Our landlord sold the building. We have to move in 60 days, and we have to start looking for apartments again.
Your advice: empathy first + an expression if it fits
PROBLEM 5
My small bakery almost closed last winter. Now we have more customers, but I'm still worried about January.
Your advice: empathy first + an expression if it fits
PROBLEM 6
I sent a message complaining about my manager... to my manager. She hasn't replied yet.
Your advice: empathy first + an expression if it fits

Language Research Report

All five are current in American English and appropriate for A2+/B1 active use.

in a tight spot

Meaning
in a difficult situation, and it's hard to find a way out (often with little time or money)
Pronunciation
in a TIGHT SPOT
Grammar
be in a tight spot · be in a bit of a tight spot
put someone in a tight spot (= make it difficult for them)
in a tight spot financially / with money / with time
Example
The babysitter canceled an hour before my shift. I was in a real tight spot.
Collocations
in a tight spot · put someone in a tight spot · get out of a tight spot · a bit of a tight spot
Register
Neutral to casual. Fine with friends, coworkers, and your boss: "I'm in a bit of a tight spot with this deadline."
Learner mistake
NOT "in a tightly spot" (tight is an adjective) and NOT "in tight spot" (you need a).
Produce?
Yes. One of the 15 core expressions for the Final.
Authentic use
"These revolutionary changes seem to put workers in a tight spot." (The Wall Street Journal)

back to square one

Meaning
back at the beginning, because your plan or work failed; you have to start again
Pronunciation
back to SQUARE ONE
Grammar
be back to square one · go back to square one · be back at square one
Often alone as a reaction: "Well... back to square one."
No article: square one (NOT the square one)
Example
The landlord rented the apartment to someone else, so we're back to square one.
Collocations
go back to square one · be back to square one · start from square one · similar: back to the drawing board
Register
Neutral. Safe everywhere, including work meetings and with your teacher.
Learner mistake
NOT "back to the square one" (no the) and NOT "back to square first."
Produce?
Yes. Use it actively.
Authentic use
"If not, we are back to square one." (MarketWatch, 2026)

face the music

Meaning
to accept the bad results (consequences) of something YOU did wrong
Pronunciation
FACE the MU-sic
Grammar
have to face the music · it's time to face the music · be ready to face the music
Only face changes: faced the music, facing the music
Fixed words: NOT a music, NOT musics
Example
I missed the deadline because I didn't plan well. Tomorrow I have to face the music.
Collocations
have to face the music · time to face the music · ready to face the music
Register
Neutral to casual. A little old-fashioned but still common, often a bit humorous. Use it for YOUR mistakes, not bad luck (illness, weather, accidents). Saying "You need to face the music" to someone can sound harsh.
Learner mistake
NOT for bad luck: "It rained on her wedding, so she faced the music." (wrong). NOT "face the musics."
Produce?
Yes, about your own mistakes. Be careful when you say it to someone else.
Authentic use
"And then I'll have to face the music." (Slate, 2023)

turn the corner

Meaning
to get past the worst part of a problem; things start to get better
Pronunciation
TURN the COR-ner
Grammar
turn the corner (most common in the U.S.) · turn a corner (also used)
have finally turned the corner · be starting to turn the corner
Also literal: turn the corner onto Main Street. Context tells you!
Example
It was a hard year for the store, but we've finally turned the corner.
Collocations
finally turn the corner · start to turn the corner · turn the corner on (a problem)
Register
Neutral. Common at work, in the news, and with friends.
Learner mistake
NOT "turned corner" (you need the or a). Use it when things START to improve, not when everything is perfect.
Produce?
Yes. One of the 15 core expressions for the Final.
Authentic use
"...confident Stellantis will turn the corner" (The Wall Street Journal, 2026)

out of the woods

Meaning
safe; the difficult or dangerous part is over. Very often negative: not out of the woods yet = better, but there may still be problems.
Pronunciation
OUT of the WOODS · woods rhymes with "goods"
Grammar
be out of the woods
not out of the woods yet (very common)
Always plural: woods
Example
The rain stopped, but we're not out of the woods yet. Another storm is coming tonight.
Collocations
not out of the woods yet · finally out of the woods · not quite out of the woods
Register
Neutral. You will hear it a lot in news about business, weather, and health.
Learner mistake
NOT "out of the wood" (that's British). In American English: woods.
Produce?
Yes. The negative form (not ... yet) is especially useful.
Authentic use
"Intel is not out of the woods yet." (MarketWatch, 2026)

Teaching decisions

  • turn a corner → turn the corner. Merriam-Webster's idiom entry is turn the corner: "to get past the most difficult area or period in something and begin to improve." Turn a corner is an accepted alternative. The syllabus and the Final list turn a corner, so both forms are accepted on every auto-check and in the Final.
  • out of the woods is taught with its very common negative form, not out of the woods yet. Out of the wood is British, so it's treated as an error in American English.
  • face the music is still widely used, but a little old-fashioned. Merriam-Webster defines it as meeting an unpleasant situation or the consequences of one's actions; most everyday use is about consequences of your own mistakes. Teach students to use it about themselves and to avoid it for bad luck or illness.
  • back to square one: no article; Merriam-Webster also lists back at square one. Similar: back to the drawing board.
  • in a tight spot: common pattern put someone in a tight spot (Merriam-Webster Learner's: "You've put me in a tight spot").

Listening: why original voicemails?

Real voicemails aren't publicly available, and news clips with these idioms are too fast for A2+. The three voicemails are original scripts recorded with synthetic American voices (25–37 seconds each). They model real voicemail features: greeting, "it's ___", apology, request, "call me back". Marcus's message also models professional register with a manager. The audio is built into both files and sent as MP3s.

Teacher Notes

Changes from the old Week 8 worksheet (Sasha's packet)

  • The old mini-dialogues and Complete the Dialogue story use a USCIS rejection, a sick child, and immigration status ("60 days left on my status"), and the Talk About It questions ask about personal hardship since moving here. The syllabus says these must be opt-in. This set uses neutral situations (locked keys, a lost file, a broken ladder) and keeps one optional "Important Application" card with a real-or-invented choice.
  • Fix the Mistake item 2 had two errors ("he have to face the musics"). Fix-It Garage has exactly one error per sentence.
  • "turn a corner" is taught as "turn the corner" (the more common American form), with both accepted.

Personal topics

Every story and role-play can be real or invented. The Advice Hotline and Problem Wall use given problems only. Some problems mention money (rent, a late fee) in a neutral way; you can remove a poster if it feels too close for your group.

Assessment connection

  • Final: in a tight spot and turn a corner are core expressions. The Advice Hotline rehearses the spontaneous exchange format.
  • Week 10 recycles Weeks 7–8: keep the Hotline cards and timeline strips.

Sharing

  • Upload week8-student.html to GitHub as usual; the print PDF is for paper students.
  • Keep week8-teacher.html private (answer key).
